docs.description: a passive effect measures layout, which reads back a frame the user has already seen
docs.why: `getBoundingClientRect` and friends force the browser to flush pending style and layout. Done in `useEffect`, that happens *after* the browser has painted, so a state write derived from the measurement shows the user one frame at the old position and then jumps. `useLayoutEffect` runs before paint, which is why the same code there is correct — the fix is the hook, not the measurement.
docs.fix: Move the measurement, and the write it feeds, into `useLayoutEffect`. If the value is only used for analytics or logging, keep `useEffect` and do not write state from it.

rules.message: this passive effect calls {c.name} — layout measured after paint, so anything derived from it shows one stale frame

docs.description: an effect acquires a resource and no call in it gives the resource back
docs.why: `observer.observe`, `URL.createObjectURL`, `getUserMedia` and `socket.join` each hand out something the browser or the server keeps until it is told otherwise. None of them is a callback registration, so `missing-cleanup` never looks at them — and it goes silent entirely as soon as the effect returns *any* cleanup, however unrelated. The rule below asks the narrower, checkable question: does any call in this effect, cleanup included, undo the acquisition?
docs.fix: Return a cleanup that calls the matching release — `disconnect`/`unobserve`, `revokeObjectURL`, `track.stop()`, `leave` — for every acquisition the setup performed.
docs.example: useEffect(() => { const ro = new ResizeObserver(cb); ro.observe(el); }, []);  // never disconnected

rules.message: this effect calls {c.name} and nothing in it gives that back — no release call appears anywhere in the effect or its cleanup

docs.description: the render body performs an imperative navigation
docs.why: Rendering must be a pure function of props and state. A `router.push` in the body runs during render — twice under StrictMode, and again on every re-render that reaches the same branch — so the history stack grows, the navigation can fire while React is still committing, and a concurrent render that React throws away has already had its side effect.
docs.fix: Navigate from an effect, or return a declarative redirect element. A guard clause that renders `null` and navigates in `useEffect` is the usual shape.
docs.example: function Page({ user }) { if (!user) router.push('/login'); return <App/>; }

rules.message: {anchor.receiver}.{anchor.name} runs during render — move it into an effect or return a redirect element

docs.description: the render body runs a known-expensive call on every render
docs.why: A `JSON.parse` of a large payload, a `sort` of a long list, a `new Intl.*` formatter: each runs on every render, including the ones caused by an unrelated state change, and each is invisible in a profile until the list is big. The identity cost is separate and worse — a fresh array from `sort` defeats every memo below it.
docs.fix: Wrap it in `useMemo` keyed on the inputs it actually reads, or hoist it out of the component if the inputs are module-level.
docs.example: function Table({ rowsJson }) { const rows = JSON.parse(rowsJson); … }

rules.message: {anchor.name} runs in the render body on every render — wrap it in useMemo keyed on its inputs

docs.description: the render body mints a brand-new identifier or timestamp on every render
docs.why: `crypto.randomUUID()`, `Math.random()` and `Date.now()` in a render body produce a different value every render. Used as a list `key` that remounts the whole row — losing focus, scroll, input state and every child effect — and used as a prop it defeats memoization the same way a fresh object would. The engine has no value-provenance verdict (#127's neighbour), so this names the mint sites rather than tracing where the value lands: a component that mints one and uses it only for a log message is reported too.
docs.fix: Key rows by a stable id from the data. If an id genuinely does not exist, mint it once where the data is created — not during render.

rules.message: {anchor.name} mints a new value on every render — as a key or a prop that remounts or re-renders everything below it

docs.description: a state slot no render-phase read ever consumes
docs.why: A slot that no render-phase read consumes is a pure re-render generator: every write commits a new render that produces the same output. The classic is a `scrollY` or `mousePosition` slot kept for a feature that was removed, still driven at event rate. Two weakenings to know. The verdict is an ABSENCE — a read the walk could not enter (a closure nothing calls, a read past the depth cap) leaves no row — so this over-reports and never certifies. And a render-phase read is not proof the value reaches the *output*: a slot read during render and then dropped still silences the rule, because there is no reachability verdict yet (#127's second half).
docs.fix: Delete the slot, or move the value into a `useRef` if something outside the render still needs it.
docs.example: const [scrollY, setScrollY] = useState(0);  // setScrollY on every scroll, scrollY never rendered

rules.message: state {anchor.name} is written but no render-phase read of it is visible — every write costs a render that changes nothing
